subcomponents.title: Uses stable identities and appropriate grouped-scene architecture

criteria.rationale: Grouping: all nine step modules set groupKey 'sample' and Scene SampleScene. In steps.ts, sceneKey(step) returns `group:${groupKey}:${sceneId(Scene)}`, so all nine steps get one key. Stage.tsx uses that value as the key of its motion.div and renders <Scene payload index/> inside it, so stepping between them re-renders the same mounted SampleScene with a new payload. Identity: entities.ts defines the presentation-owned GEOMETRY namespace (EntityId = keyof GEOMETRY) with one fixed rectangle per entity. SampleScene's g(id) and line(id) pass those ids as the `id` prop. SampleScene renders each shown entity under Appear key={id}, inside a SceneLayer with an AnimatePresence. Box, Label, SymbolChip, Emphasis and Frame all render PositionedNode with {...props} or {...rest}, so `id` reaches it. PositionedNode sets layoutId={id} with `layout`, so the kit's layout mechanism morphs a persisting entity in place. Stage wraps the scene in a LayoutGroup. The Arrow entities (you-skill, link-1..3, plug, verify-link, modify) take the same id from line(id). Arrow has no layoutId, but it sits under Appear key={id} and animates its path `d`, so the persisting element's geometry updates in place. All ids in VIEWS and LAYERS are consumed by rendered elements. Each step's visible list extends the previous step's list, so entities persist across steps.

criteria.rationale: I rule judge A's fail. The guidance says to confirm that public inputs the demo consumes are actually used, and to score a dead or misleading contract under this criterion. The demo's own payload contract is misleading. In entities.ts, SamplePayload.visible is documented as 'Entities on screen at this step, in draw order.' It turns payload.visible into a Set (`shown`) and draws entities in the fixed LAYERS[].ids order, filtering by membership only. Step 4 shows the mismatch. subcomponents.title: Entity transitions and persistent grouped scenes

criteria.rationale: Every positioned primitive is a motion.div with layout and layoutId set to the entity id. A changed x/y/size or content therefore animates in place over LAYOUT_T. The Appear wrapper stays mounted across grouped steps, so the node is not remounted.

judging basis: consensus-pass

criteria.rationale: The requirement is met. Between two ungrouped steps, the kit's transition keeps both scenes mounted together, and the primitive that renders a persisting entity stays visible while it morphs. `sceneKey` gives ungrouped steps distinct keys (`step:${id}`), so the scene remounts. Stage wraps the scene in `<AnimatePresence initial={false}>` with no `mode`, so it uses the default sync mode. Both scene wrappers are `position: absolute` (taken out of layout flow) inside one shared LayoutGroup. They cross-fade over the same ENTER_T with no delay, so the outgoing copy stays rendered while the incoming copy mounts at once. The entity primitive `Box` renders through `PositionedNode`, which is a `motion.div` with `layout` and `layoutId={id}` and a LAYOUT_T layout transition. It has no initial opacity of 0 and no entrance delay. The incoming copy therefore shares its identity with the outgoing copy and is projected from the old position, size and content to the new ones in place, so it does not vanish and reappear. This matches judge A. Judges B and C both rely on `Appear` (initial opacity 0, delay ENTER_DELAY = 0.6 s, longer than the 0.4 s ENTER_T fade). That is accurate about `Appear`, but it does not decide this requirement. `Appear` is the kit's opt-in newcomer wrapper, not the primitive that renders a persisting entity, and the persisting-entity path (`Box`/`PositionedNode`) applies no hidden or delayed start. The sample's wrapping of every entity in `Appear` only ever runs inside one shared group: every sample step has groupKey 'sample' and the same SampleScene, as sample.test.tsx asserts. So the delivered sample never produces the ungrouped transition B and C describe, and the guidance's failure pattern (a primitive that hides the incoming copy, with the delay applied to the layout animation as well) does not hold for the entity primitive. B's point that the incoming scene wrapper starts at opacity 0 does not show a gap either. That wrapper fades in over ENTER_T with no delay while the outgoing wrapper fades out over the same span, so a copy is rendered throughout the morph. C's point that no test covers the ungrouped morph is not decisive: the guidance asks for the transition mechanism plus the entity primitives, not a focused test.

Every transition with i > 0 waits until getAttribute('data-step-index') === String(i) (lines 181-185). This compares strings and never converts with Number(), so a missing or non-numeric index never matches. On timeout, lines 186-189 throw PhaseError('render', 'transition did not advance: data-step-index is X, expected i', i). Any other render error is wrapped as a render-phase failure (lines 202-204). subcomponents.title: Verification tooling robustness

criteria.rationale: In both the repository and bootstrap-template copies, startPreview (scripts/lib/preview.mjs:58-88) spawns the Vite server directly: `process.execPath node_modules/vite/bin/vite.js preview` with `detached: true`. There is no npm or npx wrapper. stop() sends SIGTERM and then SIGKILL to the whole process group (`process.kill(-child.pid, …)`) and waits on the child's 'exit' promise. If the readiness wait fails, startPreview calls stop() before rethrowing. In verify's renderPhase (verify.mjs:145-209) and inspect's runInspect (inspect-presentation.mjs:207-239), `chromium.launch()` and all later work run inside a try block whose finally calls `await browser?.close()` and then `await preview.stop()`. Success, a failing check (PhaseError), a browser launch failure and any later error all pass through that finally. The template copies have the same code at the same lines. Judge C fails the criterion because verify's onSignal handler calls process.exit(130) on SIGINT/SIGTERM without stopping the preview. That handler does exist (verify.mjs:234-236). votes.rationale: Grouping: all nine step modules set groupKey 'sample' and Scene SampleScene. In steps.ts, sceneKey(step) returns `group:${groupKey}:${sceneId(Scene)}`, so all nine steps get one key. Stage.tsx uses that value as the key of its motion.div and renders <Scene payload index/> inside it, so stepping between them re-renders the same mounted SampleScene with a new payload. Identity: entities.ts defines the presentation-owned GEOMETRY namespace (EntityId = keyof GEOMETRY) with one fixed rectangle per entity. SampleScene's g(id) and line(id) pass those ids as the `id` prop. SampleScene renders each shown entity under Appear key={id}, inside a SceneLayer with an AnimatePresence. Box, Label, SymbolChip, Emphasis and Frame all render PositionedNode with {...props} or {...rest}, so `id` reaches it. PositionedNode sets layoutId={id} with `layout`, so the kit's layout mechanism morphs a persisting entity in place. Stage wraps the scene in a LayoutGroup. The Arrow entities (you-skill, link-1..3, plug, verify-link, modify) take the same id from line(id). Arrow has no layoutId, but it sits under Appear key={id} and animates its path `d`, so the persisting element's geometry updates in place. All ids in VIEWS and LAYERS are consumed by rendered elements. Each step's visible list extends the previous step's list, so entities persist across steps.

SampleScene is the Scene for every step, and it ignores that order: it turns payload.visible into a Set and then draws entities by the fixed LAYERS[].ids order. Step 4 shows the mismatch. The review guidance says to check that consumed public inputs and shared constants are really used, and it files a dead or misleading contract under demo-clear-code-boundaries. The pass rationale is right that the title is consumed (Talk's title reaches Presentation's aria-label), but that does not fix this separate misleading contract, so the pass does not stand.

result.rationale: I rule judge A's fail. The guidance says to confirm that public inputs the demo consumes are actually used, and to score a dead or misleading contract under this criterion. The demo's own payload contract is misleading. In entities.ts, SamplePayload.visible is documented as 'Entities on screen at this step, in draw order.' SampleScene is the Scene for every step, and it does not follow that order. It turns payload.visible into a Set (`shown`) and draws entities in the fixed LAYERS[].ids order, filtering by membership only. Step 4 shows the mismatch. Its visible list is built from step3 ([..., 'tray', 'card-1', 'link-1', 'morph-1']) with 'card-2', 'card-3', 'card-4', ... appended after it. So the contract says link-1 and morph-1 draw before card-2. The tray layer actually draws card-1, card-2, card-3, card-4 before link-1 and morph-1. Draw order (DOM order) is exactly what the documented contract promises, and it is ignored. Judges B and C correctly found that the title contract is consumed: Talk passes title, and Presentation renders aria-label={title}. They also found that OVERLAYS is used by tests/unit/sample.test.tsx. Both observations are accurate, but neither looked at the visible/draw-order contract. A valid title path does not cure a separate misleading contract, so their reasons do not decide the requirement.

scene-kit.rationale: The requirement is met. Between two ungrouped steps, the kit's transition keeps both scenes mounted together, and the primitive that renders a persisting entity stays visible while it morphs. `sceneKey` gives ungrouped steps distinct keys (`step:${id}`), so the scene remounts. Stage wraps the scene in `<AnimatePresence initial={false}>` with no `mode`, so it uses the default sync mode. Both scene wrappers are `position: absolute` (taken out of layout flow) inside one shared LayoutGroup. They cross-fade over the same ENTER_T with no delay, so the outgoing copy stays rendered while the incoming copy mounts at once. The entity primitive `Box` renders through `PositionedNode`, which is a `motion.div` with `layout` and `layoutId={id}` and a LAYOUT_T layout transition. It has no initial opacity of 0 and no entrance delay. The incoming copy therefore shares its identity with the outgoing copy and is projected from the old position, size and content to the new ones in place, so it does not vanish and reappear. This matches judge A. Judges B and C both rely on `Appear` (initial opacity 0, delay ENTER_DELAY = 0.6 s, longer than the 0.4 s ENTER_T fade). That is accurate about `Appear`, but it does not decide this requirement. `Appear` is the kit's opt-in newcomer wrapper, not the primitive that renders a persisting entity, and the persisting-entity path (`Box`/`PositionedNode`) applies no hidden or delayed start. The sample's wrapping of every entity in `Appear` only ever runs inside one shared group: every sample step has groupKey 'sample' and the same SampleScene, as sample.test.tsx asserts. So the delivered sample never produces the ungrouped transition B and C describe, and the guidance's failure pattern (a primitive that hides the incoming copy, with the delay applied to the layout animation as well) does not hold for the entity primitive. B's point that the incoming scene wrapper starts at opacity 0 does not show a gap either. That wrapper fades in over ENTER_T with no delay while the outgoing wrapper fades out over the same span, so a copy is rendered throughout the morph. C's point that no test covers the ungrouped morph is not decisive: the guidance asks for the transition mechanism plus the entity primitives, not a focused test.

votes.rationale: The kit's primitives are typed from the element props (HTMLMotionProps<'div'>, SVGProps, HTMLAttributes) and strip kit-only props such as `icon` and `kind`. But they apply their identity hooks before the caller's props, so a caller can override them. PositionedNode sets `layoutId={id}`, `data-presentation-node` and `data-presentation-id` and only then spreads `{...rest}`. A caller-supplied `data-presentation-id` or `data-presentation-node` (data-* attributes are accepted in JSX) replaces the kit's. Arrow sets `data-presentation-node="arrow"` and `data-presentation-id` before `{...(rest as object)}`, which also casts the props to bypass typing. Appear sets `data-presentation-appear` before `{...rest}`, and SceneLayer sets `data-presentation-scene-layer` before `{...rest}`. The requirement that identity hooks go after caller props is not met.

result.rationale: I side with judges A and B. None of the delivered tests sleeps for a fixed time before asserting. The four slow tests (e2e-001, e2e-002, int-001, int-002) never drive Playwright themselves. Each one runs `npm run verify` or the inspect script through the synchronous helper `run()` (spawnSync). Only after that process has exited do the tests assert, on its exit code, its printed output, the files it wrote and the leftover processes. The only `setTimeout` in e2e-002 is a string injected into app code to raise a page error; the test does not wait on it. The unit test `inspect-script.test.ts` uses a fake page whose `waitForTimeout` and `waitForFunction` only record calls, so nothing sleeps. The jsdom unit tests that wait for something (scene.test.tsx, routing.test.tsx) use `waitFor(() => expect(...))`, which polls observable state: the scene count, the opacity, the loaded text and the presentation root. Inside the verify script that these tests run, each step first goes through `page.waitForFunction` on `data-step-index` with a timeout, and only then runs the settle delay. So the step check waits on state, not on a sleep. Judge C's reason does not decide the requirement. C cites the VERIFY_SETTLE_MS and `--settle` values passed by e2e-001 and int-002, and inspect's `waitForTimeout(settleMs)`. Those are settings passed to the verification scripts, not sleeps inside a test. The settle delay runs only after the state wait on data-step-index, as verify.mjs lines 176-192 show. int-002 checks the recorded settle values in captures.json after the subprocess has finished; it does not sleep in place of waiting for state. The guidance also lists longer fixed settle delays as validator noise.

result.rationale: Fail. The record leaves a substantial share of behaviour the environment allowed unexercised. (1) Motion behaviour: the six scenarios under 'Stable entities morph across steps' (persisting entity morphs, new entity enters after others settle, departing entity exits) and 'Persistent grouped scenes' (grouped steps update in place, continuing entities are not faded) have no motion observation. The log shows only settled screenshots and a note that 'all earlier entities persist through step 7'. That is the weaker persistence-instead-of-motion check the criterion says does not cover a scenario. Departing entities are never observed. The log excludes mid-transition morph capture as 'unnecessary' or 'beyond the planned three-step budget', which is a choice, not an environmental impediment, so it counts against coverage. (2) Verification failure paths: the console/page-error, step-error and malformed-sample (missing sample) scenarios were deliberately not run because 'the relevant tests own these paths', and the handoff confirms those test suites were not run either. (3) 'Controls keep their keys' was planned ('focused-control key handling') but appears in neither the navigation observations nor the 'Deliberately not exercised' list, so this undisclosed omission counts fully. Judges A and B passed by calling the gaps modest and noting the morph omission was disclosed and observed via static screenshots. votes.rationale: The verifier reserves a fresh port with freePort and uses --strictPort, but readiness comes from HTTP polling of that port. first_results.rationale: I rule judge A's fail. The guidance says to confirm that public inputs the demo consumes are actually used, and to score a dead or misleading contract under this criterion. The demo's own payload contract is misleading. In entities.ts, SamplePayload.visible is documented as 'Entities on screen at this step, in draw order.' SampleScene is the Scene for every step, and it does not follow that order. It turns payload.visible into a Set (`shown`) and draws entities in the fixed LAYERS[].ids order, filtering by membership only. Step 4 shows the mismatch. Its visible list is built from step3 ([..., 'tray', 'card-1', 'link-1', 'morph-1']) with 'card-2', 'card-3', 'card-4', ... appended after it. So the contract says link-1 and morph-1 draw before card-2. The tray layer actually draws card-1, card-2, card-3, card-4 before link-1 and morph-1. Draw order (DOM order) is exactly what the documented contract promises, and it is ignored. Judges B and C correctly found that the title contract is consumed: Talk passes title, and Presentation renders aria-label={title}. They also found that OVERLAYS is used by tests/unit/sample.test.tsx. Both observations are accurate, but neither looked at the visible/draw-order contract. A valid title path does not cure a separate misleading contract, so their reasons do not decide the requirement.

Between two ungrouped steps, the kit's transition keeps both scenes mounted together, and the primitive that renders a persisting entity stays visible while it morphs. `sceneKey` gives ungrouped steps distinct keys (`step:${id}`), so the scene remounts. audit_results.rationale: The criterion is met. It asks whether, between two consecutive steps that do not share a scene group, the kit's step transition keeps both steps' entities present together, and whether the kit's entity primitives keep a persisting entity visible while it morphs in place. The quoted code shows both. steps.ts:45-49 gives ungrouped steps distinct keys (`step:${id}`), so each one remounts its scene. Stage.tsx:49-61 wraps the scene in AnimatePresence with no `mode`, which means the default sync mode. Each scene wrapper is position:absolute (line 57), so the outgoing step is out of layout flow. The incoming wrapper fades in over ENTER_T with no delay while the outgoing one fades out over the same span. So both scenes are mounted at once, which scene.test.tsx:74-80 checks: more than one [data-presentation-scene] is present after advancing between different groups. The entity primitives (Box → PositionedNode, Box.tsx:10-17 and PositionedNode.tsx:36-47) render a motion.div with `layout`, `layoutId={id}` and a LAYOUT_T layout transition. They have no initial opacity of 0 and no entrance delay, and scene.test.tsx:127-138 confirms this for every positioned primitive. The incoming copy therefore shares its identity with the outgoing copy, which is still rendered, and is projected from its old state to its new one. This does not match the failure pattern the guidance names: a mode="wait" transition, or entity primitives with a hidden start and a delay as long as the step transition that also applies to the layout animation. The delayed hidden start belongs to Appear (Appear.tsx:17-24), an opt-in newcomer wrapper. It does not render the persisting entity and has no layout or layoutId. The delivered sample uses Appear only inside one shared group (sample.test.tsx:30-38), so the sample never produces an ungrouped transition. Both scene wrappers fade over the same ENTER_T with no delay, so a copy of the entity is rendered throughout the transition. The guidance asks for the transition mechanism plus the entity primitives, not a focused test.

first_results.rationale: The requirement is met. A step that fails to render or advance makes verification exit non-zero and names the failing step. Missing or invalid hooks are never counted as progress. In renderPhase (scripts/verify.mjs:170-174), the step count is read with Number(getAttribute('data-step-count')). If it is not an integer of at least 1, a render PhaseError at step 0 is thrown, so a missing count (Number(null) is 0) or a non-numeric count (NaN) can never lead to stepping through zero steps and passing. Every transition with i > 0 waits until getAttribute('data-step-index') === String(i) (lines 181-185). This compares strings and never converts with Number(), so a missing or non-numeric index never matches. On timeout, lines 186-189 throw PhaseError('render', 'transition did not advance: data-step-index is X, expected i', i). Any other render error is wrapped as a render-phase failure (lines 202-204). The main block prints 'VERIFY FAILED phase=<phase> step=<n>' and sets exitCode = 1 (lines 240-244). The focused test in tests/slow/e2e-002.test.ts:67-76 edits usePresentationNav so the index stops advancing at 2. It runs `npm run verify` on a copy of the app and asserts a non-zero exit and 'VERIFY FAILED phase=render step=3: transition did not advance: data-step-index is 2, expected 3'. Judge B's point is correct but does not decide the criterion. Step 0 is the initial state, not a transition, so its index is never accepted as progress. The guidance's example (Number(null) === 0 on the first step) describes a transition check that converts a missing hook into a passing number. This verifier has no such check: if the index hook were missing, the first transition (step 1) would fail, because null !== '1'. This rules with judges A and C.

They call spawnSync through helpers.run (tests/slow/helpers.ts:23-32), which returns only after the verify or inspect script has exited, and then assert on the exit code, the printed output and the written artifacts. Inside the scripts, every step change is awaited by polling the observable data-step-index with page.waitForFunction and a timeout (verify.mjs:176-191, inspect-presentation.mjs:163-171), and mode changes are polled the same way (verify.mjs:121-129). Judge C fails the criterion because the tests set VERIFY_SETTLE_MS or --settle and the scripts then sleep a fixed interval. In inspect it is the helper's own settle-before-screenshot feature, which int-002 tests rather than relies on as a wait (int-002.test.ts:68-77). The guidance also treats longer fixed settle delays as validator noise. C's reason therefore does not show a test that sleeps instead of waiting for state, so judges A and B are right.

results.rationale: I side with judges A and B. None of the delivered tests sleeps for a fixed time before asserting. The four slow tests (e2e-001, e2e-002, int-001, int-002) never drive Playwright themselves. Each one runs `npm run verify` or the inspect script through the synchronous helper `run()` (spawnSync). Only after that process has exited do the tests assert, on its exit code, its printed output, the files it wrote and the leftover processes. The only `setTimeout` in e2e-002 is a string injected into app code to raise a page error; the test does not wait on it. The unit test `inspect-script.test.ts` uses a fake page whose `waitForTimeout` and `waitForFunction` only record calls, so nothing sleeps. The jsdom unit tests that wait for something (scene.test.tsx, routing.test.tsx) use `waitFor(() => expect(...))`, which polls observable state: the scene count, the opacity, the loaded text and the presentation root. Inside the verify script that these tests run, each step first goes through `page.waitForFunction` on `data-step-index` with a timeout, and only then runs the settle delay. So the step check waits on state, not on a sleep. Judge C's reason does not decide the requirement. C cites the VERIFY_SETTLE_MS and `--settle` values passed by e2e-001 and int-002, and inspect's `waitForTimeout(settleMs)`. Those are settings passed to the verification scripts, not sleeps inside a test. The settle delay runs only after the state wait on data-step-index, as verify.mjs lines 176-192 show. int-002 checks the recorded settle values in captures.json after the subprocess has finished; it does not sleep in place of waiting for state. The guidance also lists longer fixed settle delays as validator noise.

result.rationale: I side with judges A and B. None of the delivered tests sleeps for a fixed time before asserting. The four slow tests (e2e-001, e2e-002, int-001, int-002) never drive Playwright themselves. Each one runs `npm run verify` or the inspect script through the synchronous helper `run()` (spawnSync). Only after that process has exited do the tests assert, on its exit code, its printed output, the files it wrote and the leftover processes. Inside the verify script that these tests run, each step first goes through `page.waitForFunction` on `data-step-index` with a timeout, and only then runs the settle delay. So the step check waits on state, not on a sleep. Judge C's reason does not decide the requirement. C cites the VERIFY_SETTLE_MS and `--settle` values passed by e2e-001 and int-002, and inspect's `waitForTimeout(settleMs)`. Those are settings passed to the verification scripts, not sleeps inside a test. The settle delay runs only after the state wait on data-step-index, as verify.mjs lines 176-192 show. int-002 checks the recorded settle values in captures.json after the subprocess has finished; it does not sleep in place of waiting for state. ## Monorepo build anchor scope during partial scaffolding (acceptance round 0)

- **Question:** In AT-001's non-empty monorepo with only a root build anchor, does “scaffold only missing anchors” reuse the root build anchor for the app under `presentations/`, or does the self-contained nested app need a second build anchor of its own?

- **Evidence:** In a disposable monorepo with a valid root build anchor, `resolve` targeted `presentations/` and reported all three anchors missing for that target. The unconfirmed apply refused to write; after confirmation it created a self-contained nested app with its own build setup while preserving root files. See `scratch/acceptance-test/mono-build-no-confirm.err` and `scratch/acceptance-test/mono-build-apply.out`.

- **Options:** Reuse the root build setup and add only kit/index files under `presentations/`; or treat the nested self-contained app as an independent target and add its own build setup, leaving the root build alone.

- **Consequence:** The choice changes what “partial scaffold” means in monorepos and whether duplicate Vite/React configuration is expected. The design emphasizes a self-contained nested app; AT-001 says the partial monorepo has only a build anchor and should preserve existing setup while adding missing infrastructure. Human acceptance should reconcile that wording.
## Diagram text is too small to read on a narrow portrait viewport (acceptance finding AS-001)

- **Question:** At 390 × 844 the fixed 880 × 380 canvas scales to about 0.41, so the sample's 11 to 13 px diagram text renders at roughly 4.5 to 5.5 px. On the dense step 7 the labels cannot be read. A phone viewer would clearly call that broken. Is it a defect to fix, or the intended result of the approved fit-scaling?

- **Requirement:** evolving-scene-presentations, "Fixed-canvas fit scaling": the diagram is composed in a fixed canvas and "scaled uniformly to fit the available viewport, so the composition does not reflow". The default canvas is 880 × 380. In the same spec, "Uniform scaling on resize" says it scales "without reflowing its internal composition". presentation-skill, "Visual composition is inspected": content fits the fixed canvas, intentional overlaps stay readable, and nothing collides with chrome. The test plan also expects important content to be "readable" at the narrow width.
- **Ruling:** I found no fix inside the approved definition, so I made no change. This is a decision needed from the user.

- **Observed behavior follows the spec:** With a width-bound uniform scale and no reflow, a diagram 880 px wide on a 390 px screen is about 0.4 of its design size. Composition fits, with no overlap or chrome collision. That is what "Fixed-canvas fit scaling" and "Uniform scaling on resize" require.

- **Why I won't resolve it silently:** The spec's wording is "fits", and the test plan's "readable" is stricter. The two cannot both be met for dense steps on a portrait phone without changing something the definition fixes.
1. Leave as it is and accept small text on narrow portrait phones. Documented as a limit of the fixed-canvas model.

2. Presentation-side change inside the approved model: enlarge the sample's diagram text where geometry allows. This helps only a little: doubling the sizes gives about 9 px effective at best, and the 100 × 100 step cards have no room for it. It would need visual re-inspection, which this step cannot do.

3. Let narrow viewports show the canvas at a larger minimum scale with horizontal panning, or use a different canvas per breakpoint. This reflows or changes the composition, so it contradicts "does not reflow" and "uniformly scaled" and changes the approved model.
4. Add an advisory helper warning for text whose effective rendered size is under a threshold. This is not required by the spec, and it would flag the sample today.

- **Rationale:** Options 1 and 2 stay inside the approved behavior, and 2 gives a marginal gain I cannot check without a browser. Options 3 and 4 change approved behavior or scope. Choosing among them is a product decision.

- **Pending decision:** Yes. The user should choose one of options 1 to 4, or say narrow portrait readability is out of scope for the sample. My recommendation is option 1 plus option 2 later as presentation polish.
- **Question:** How much must anchor detection establish before it is "contract-level", as opposed to only spotting names?

- Today `detectAnchors` marks the scene kit present when some source exports a function or const named `Presentation` and any file in that directory subtree contains the token `AnimatePresence`. It checks nothing about the step types, navigation, modes, chrome or fit scaling.
- It marks the index present when any source has an unquoted `slug:` and `load:` plus `import(`, and does not check that anything routes from it.
- The `withKit` test fixture is `export const Presentation = () => null` plus a file that mentions `AnimatePresence`, and the tests treat that as a complete kit.
- A registry written as `{ 'slug': 'a', 'load': () => import('./a') }` is not detected.
- Is this a compliant heuristic, or a silently weaker detection that L-33, L-35, L-36 and I-31 should flag?

- **Requirement:** presentation-skill, "Self-bootstrapping scaffold". The scene kit anchor is the reusable engine: the `Step`/`Scene` step contract, the stage/host that mounts the active step and runs entity morphs, present/browse navigation, and the chrome and fit-scale canvas. The index anchor is the registry that maps each presentation to its own route. "Detection is contract-level, keyed on the presence of these anchors rather than a byte-identical scaffold, so cosmetic differences (file naming, formatting, extra dependencies) do not trigger re-scaffolding." The scenarios "Already scaffolded" and "Partial scaffold" depend on detection being correct.

- **Ruling:** A static, heuristic detector is compliant in kind. It cannot prove runtime behavior, and the definition asks for "presence" of the anchors and does not ask for proof. The current detector is not compliant in how much it checks, and it should be flagged. The false positive on the stub kit and the false negative on a differently quoted registry both conflict with the definition. L-33, L-35, L-36 and I-31 should not pass as they stand.
- **Scene kit minimum:** The kit counts as present only when its contract facets are all recognized by what the code provides, not by one name. The facets are:
2. an exported presentation host that mounts the active step through a stage doing presence and layout-group handling;
5. chrome (caption and table of contents or equivalent);
- Each facet may be recognized by a token-level or structural signal, anywhere in the host's own module graph or directory, and not by an exact file name.
- A host that is a stub, or has only some of the facets, counts as the kit missing. A missing facet is reported as such.
- Extra files and differing names or formatting must not change the result.
- **Index minimum:** The index counts as present when two things hold.
1. A module holds a registry of entries, each with a slug, a title and a lazy-loaded presentation.
2. Something routes from it: another source imports that module and uses the slug against the path.
- Quoted or unquoted keys, single or double quotes, any formatting, and any file location must be accepted. Cosmetic differences must not trigger re-scaffolding.

- **Which way to err:** A false positive skips the scaffold and leaves the project unable to render. A false negative adds files without overwriting any. Neither is acceptable for cosmetic differences, so detection should be precise on the structural facets. For doubtful cases the skill's build and render self-check is the backstop, and it must not be treated as a substitute for the facet check.

- **Test consequence:** A fixture that is an empty `Presentation` plus an `AnimatePresence` mention is not a valid "complete kit". The eight-combinations tests need fixtures that meet all facets. They also need negative cases for a stub kit, a kit missing one facet, and a registry with quoted keys, in another file, or with another layout.

- **Rationale:** The definition's own words are "contract-level" and "cosmetic differences ... do not trigger re-scaffolding". A name plus one token is what the definition rules out, so the stub kit is a false positive by its own standard. Static checks cannot prove the engine works, and the definition does not ask them to. Requiring every facet and a routed consumer is the smallest reading that stays about the contract.
- **Pending decision:** None. No requirement changes. Flagging the current detector as weaker than the definition is the ruling, not a decision to ask for.
## Registering into a detected index that differs from the canonical one

- **Question:** When detection finds an index at a different path or format, must the workflow still create and register the new presentation in it, without assuming the canonical path and format? Or may it document the gap or hand the user manual steps? Today `createPresentation` hardcodes `src/presentations/index.ts` and needs a newline before the closing `]`, and the workflow has no manual-adaptation branch.

- **Requirement:** presentation-skill, "Create a new presentation" ("registered in the presentation index", "Existing presentations are preserved"), "Self-bootstrapping scaffold" ("Already scaffolded": skip scaffolding and go straight to creating), and "Modify an existing presentation".
- **Ruling:** The workflow must register the new presentation in the index it detected.
- **No canonical assumption:** It may not assume the canonical path or layout, and it may not report success without registering.
- **No second registry:** It may not write a duplicate canonical `index.ts` beside the real registry, or re-scaffold the index anchor, because that would break "already scaffolded".
- **Two acceptable mechanisms.** At least one must exist.
1. The helper reports the detected registry path and registers into it, tolerating quoting and formatting.

2. `SKILL.md` has a clearly stated agent step: where the helper cannot register safely, the agent makes the minimal edit to the detected registry itself, then checks the result with the build and render checks.

- **Where files go:** The new presentation folder sits next to the detected registry, and its lazy-load path is relative to that registry. The same rule applies to the modify flow, where the list of registered presentations comes from the detected index.

- **Failure handling:** A helper that cannot register must exit non-zero with a clear message, and the workflow must then fall through to the agent step. It must not quietly create files and leave the presentation unreachable.
- **Current state:** The workflow has neither mechanism for a non-canonical index, so that case is a gap against the definition. This applies to L-43, L-45 and the detection rows.

- **Rationale:** Skipping re-scaffolding is only worth anything if the skill can still create and register into what it detected. Telling the user to adapt things by hand would drop a SHALL requirement. Allowing an agent edit as a fallback respects the "skill" nature of the workflow and does not demand that a script parse every possible format.
- **Pending decision:** None. Whether the helper or the agent step carries this is an implementation choice.

The design emphasizes a self-contained nested app; AT-001 says the partial monorepo has only a build anchor and should preserve existing setup while adding missing infrastructure. Human acceptance should reconcile that wording.
## Diagram text is too small to read on a narrow portrait viewport (acceptance finding AS-001)

- **Question:** At 390 × 844 the fixed 880 × 380 canvas scales to about 0.41, so the sample's 11 to 13 px diagram text renders at roughly 4.5 to 5.5 px. On the dense step 7 the labels cannot be read. A phone viewer would clearly call that broken. Is it a defect to fix, or the intended result of the approved fit-scaling?

- **Requirement:** evolving-scene-presentations, "Fixed-canvas fit scaling": the diagram is composed in a fixed canvas and "scaled uniformly to fit the available viewport, so the composition does not reflow". The default canvas is 880 × 380. In the same spec, "Uniform scaling on resize" says it scales "without reflowing its internal composition". presentation-skill, "Visual composition is inspected": content fits the fixed canvas, intentional overlaps stay readable, and nothing collides with chrome. The test plan also expects important content to be "readable" at the narrow width.
- **Ruling:** I found no fix inside the approved definition, so I made no change. This is a decision needed from the user.

- **Observed behavior follows the spec:** With a width-bound uniform scale and no reflow, a diagram 880 px wide on a 390 px screen is about 0.4 of its design size. Composition fits, with no overlap or chrome collision. That is what "Fixed-canvas fit scaling" and "Uniform scaling on resize" require.

- **Why I won't resolve it silently:** The spec's wording is "fits", and the test plan's "readable" is stricter. The two cannot both be met for dense steps on a portrait phone without changing something the definition fixes.
1. Leave as it is and accept small text on narrow portrait phones. Documented as a limit of the fixed-canvas model.

2. Presentation-side change inside the approved model: enlarge the sample's diagram text where geometry allows. This helps only a little: doubling the sizes gives about 9 px effective at best, and the 100 × 100 step cards have no room for it. It would need visual re-inspection, which this step cannot do.

3. Let narrow viewports show the canvas at a larger minimum scale with horizontal panning, or use a different canvas per breakpoint. This reflows or changes the composition, so it contradicts "does not reflow" and "uniformly scaled" and changes the approved model.
4. Add an advisory helper warning for text whose effective rendered size is under a threshold. This is not required by the spec, and it would flag the sample today.

- **Rationale:** Options 1 and 2 stay inside the approved behavior, and 2 gives a marginal gain I cannot check without a browser. Options 3 and 4 change approved behavior or scope. Choosing among them is a product decision.

- **Pending decision:** Yes. The user should choose one of options 1 to 4, or say narrow portrait readability is out of scope for the sample. My recommendation is option 1 plus option 2 later as presentation polish.
- **Question:** How much must anchor detection establish before it is "contract-level", as opposed to only spotting names?

- Today `detectAnchors` marks the scene kit present when some source exports a function or const named `Presentation` and any file in that directory subtree contains the token `AnimatePresence`. It checks nothing about the step types, navigation, modes, chrome or fit scaling.
- It marks the index present when any source has an unquoted `slug:` and `load:` plus `import(`, and does not check that anything routes from it.
- The `withKit` test fixture is `export const Presentation = () => null` plus a file that mentions `AnimatePresence`, and the tests treat that as a complete kit.
- A registry written as `{ 'slug': 'a', 'load': () => import('./a') }` is not detected.
- Is this a compliant heuristic, or a silently weaker detection that L-33, L-35, L-36 and I-31 should flag?

- **Requirement:** presentation-skill, "Self-bootstrapping scaffold". The scene kit anchor is the reusable engine: the `Step`/`Scene` step contract, the stage/host that mounts the active step and runs entity morphs, present/browse navigation, and the chrome and fit-scale canvas. The index anchor is the registry that maps each presentation to its own route. "Detection is contract-level, keyed on the presence of these anchors rather than a byte-identical scaffold, so cosmetic differences (file naming, formatting, extra dependencies) do not trigger re-scaffolding." The scenarios "Already scaffolded" and "Partial scaffold" depend on detection being correct.

- **Ruling:** A static, heuristic detector is compliant in kind. It cannot prove runtime behavior, and the definition asks for "presence" of the anchors and does not ask for proof. The current detector is not compliant in how much it checks, and it should be flagged. The false positive on the stub kit and the false negative on a differently quoted registry both conflict with the definition. L-33, L-35, L-36 and I-31 should not pass as they stand.
- **Scene kit minimum:** The kit counts as present only when its contract facets are all recognized by what the code provides, not by one name. The facets are:
2. an exported presentation host that mounts the active step through a stage doing presence and layout-group handling;
5. chrome (caption and table of contents or equivalent);
- Each facet may be recognized by a token-level or structural signal, anywhere in the host's own module graph or directory, and not by an exact file name.
- A host that is a stub, or has only some of the facets, counts as the kit missing. A missing facet is reported as such.
- Extra files and differing names or formatting must not change the result.
- **Index minimum:** The index counts as present when two things hold.
1. A module holds a registry of entries, each with a slug, a title and a lazy-loaded presentation.
2. Something routes from it: another source imports that module and uses the slug against the path.
- Quoted or unquoted keys, single or double quotes, any formatting, and any file location must be accepted. Cosmetic differences must not trigger re-scaffolding.

- **Which way to err:** A false positive skips the scaffold and leaves the project unable to render. A false negative adds files without overwriting any. Neither is acceptable for cosmetic differences, so detection should be precise on the structural facets. For doubtful cases the skill's build and render self-check is the backstop, and it must not be treated as a substitute for the facet check.

- **Test consequence:** A fixture that is an empty `Presentation` plus an `AnimatePresence` mention is not a valid "complete kit". The eight-combinations tests need fixtures that meet all facets. They also need negative cases for a stub kit, a kit missing one facet, and a registry with quoted keys, in another file, or with another layout.

- **Rationale:** The definition's own words are "contract-level" and "cosmetic differences ... do not trigger re-scaffolding". A name plus one token is what the definition rules out, so the stub kit is a false positive by its own standard. Static checks cannot prove the engine works, and the definition does not ask them to. Requiring every facet and a routed consumer is the smallest reading that stays about the contract.
- **Pending decision:** None. No requirement changes. Flagging the current detector as weaker than the definition is the ruling, not a decision to ask for.
## Registering into a detected index that differs from the canonical one

- **Question:** When detection finds an index at a different path or format, must the workflow still create and register the new presentation in it, without assuming the canonical path and format? Or may it document the gap or hand the user manual steps? Today `createPresentation` hardcodes `src/presentations/index.ts` and needs a newline before the closing `]`, and the workflow has no manual-adaptation branch.

- **Requirement:** presentation-skill, "Create a new presentation" ("registered in the presentation index", "Existing presentations are preserved"), "Self-bootstrapping scaffold" ("Already scaffolded": skip scaffolding and go straight to creating), and "Modify an existing presentation".
- **Ruling:** The workflow must register the new presentation in the index it detected.
- **No canonical assumption:** It may not assume the canonical path or layout, and it may not report success without registering.
- **No second registry:** It may not write a duplicate canonical `index.ts` beside the real registry, or re-scaffold the index anchor, because that would break "already scaffolded".
- **Two acceptable mechanisms.** At least one must exist.
1. The helper reports the detected registry path and registers into it, tolerating quoting and formatting.

2. `SKILL.md` has a clearly stated agent step: where the helper cannot register safely, the agent makes the minimal edit to the detected registry itself, then checks the result with the build and render checks.

- **Where files go:** The new presentation folder sits next to the detected registry, and its lazy-load path is relative to that registry. The same rule applies to the modify flow, where the list of registered presentations comes from the detected index.

- **Failure handling:** A helper that cannot register must exit non-zero with a clear message, and the workflow must then fall through to the agent step. It must not quietly create files and leave the presentation unreachable.
- **Current state:** The workflow has neither mechanism for a non-canonical index, so that case is a gap against the definition. This applies to L-43, L-45 and the detection rows.

- **Rationale:** Skipping re-scaffolding is only worth anything if the skill can still create and register into what it detected. Telling the user to adapt things by hand would drop a SHALL requirement. Allowing an agent edit as a fallback respects the "skill" nature of the workflow and does not demand that a script parse every possible format.
- **Pending decision:** None. Whether the helper or the agent step carries this is an implementation choice.

demo-integration.rationale: The stated contradiction holds. In entities.ts, SamplePayload.visible is documented as 'Entities on screen at this step, in draw order.' SampleScene is the Scene for every step, and it ignores that order: it turns payload.visible into a Set and then draws entities by the fixed LAYERS[].ids order. Step 4 shows the mismatch. Its visible list, built up from step1 through step3, places card-1, link-1 and morph-1 before card-2. The tray layer in SampleScene instead draws card-1, card-2, card-3, card-4 and only then link-1 and morph-1. The review guidance says to check that consumed public inputs and shared constants are really used, and it files a dead or misleading contract under demo-clear-code-boundaries. A presentation-owned payload contract that promises a draw order the renderer never follows is a misleading contract. The pass rationale is right that the title is consumed (Talk's title reaches Presentation's aria-label), but that does not fix this separate misleading contract, so the pass does not stand.
evidence: entities.ts: SamplePayload.visible carries the doc comment 'Entities on screen at this step, in draw order.'
SampleScene.tsx: const shown = new Set(payload.visible), then LAYERS.map over layer.ids filtered by shown.has(id), so the order drawn comes from LAYERS, not from visible.
SampleScene.tsx LAYERS tray ids order: tray, card-1, card-2, card-3, card-4, link-1, link-2, link-3, morph-1, morph-2, morph-3, ...
step-3.tsx appends tray, card-1, link-1, morph-1 to step2's list; step-4.tsx then appends card-2, card-3, card-4, link-2, link-3, morph-2, morph-3, so visible puts link-1 and morph-1 before card-…
Talk.tsx passes title to Presentation, which uses it as aria-label; this valid title use does not settle the misleading payload contract.

The bundled comments query reported no actionable comments; its informational comment says this draft PR was not automatically reviewed. CI evidence is therefore green for the supplied status context, with the draft review not performed.
